extracted.intended_audience: students and scholars of philosophy, logic, and the moral/social sciences; researchers interested in method and induction
extracted.subtask_description: Principles and methodological criteria for treating psychology, ethics, and social/political phenomena as scientific subjects — how to adapt inductive methods of the natural sciences to moral and social inquiry and what limits/pitfalls to expect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Methods of evidence must be empirical, not a priori
rubrics_metrics.description: Principles of Evidence and Theories of Method are not to be constructed a priori. The laws of our rational faculty, like those of every other natural agency, are only learned by seeing the agent at work.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Do not attempt to deduce rules of method from pure reason alone; study the actual successful practice of inquiry (especially in simpler cases) and generalize from that practice. The earlier achievements of science were made without conscious observance of any Scientific Method, and we learn method by observing how truth was ascertained in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Derive methods by generalizing from simpler to complex cases
rubrics_metrics.description: The way of obtaining the end is seen as it were instinctively by superior minds in some comparatively simple case, and is then, by judicious generalization, adapted to the variety of complex cases.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When developing method for difficult inquiries (e.g., moral sciences), examine procedures that worked in easier problems and generalize them carefully rather than inventing novel a priori procedures. Practical exemplification is necessary; precept without exemplification is vague and unsatisfactory.

rubrics_metrics.name: A subject is scientific if its phenomena follow constant laws
rubrics_metrics.description: Any facts are fitted, in themselves, to be a subject of science which follow one another according to constant laws, although those laws may not have been discovered, nor even be discoverable by our existing resources.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The criterion of being a science is regularity governed by laws (even if imperfectly known). Examples: meteorology and tidology are sciences despite differing degrees of exactness because their phenomena depend on laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Exact science requires accounting for all causes (major and minor)
rubrics_metrics.description: Exactness requires that phenomena be brought under laws comprehending the whole of the causes by which the phenomena are influenced, whether in a great or only in a trifling degree, and assigning to each of those causes the share of effect which really belongs to it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Distinguish exact sciences (e.g., mature astronomy) from non-exact ones (e.g., early meteorology) by whether perturbations and minor causes are understood and incorporated. Without accounting for minor causes, predictions will be approximate rather than exact.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combine exact laws of major causes with empirical approximations for minor causes
rubrics_metrics.description: By combining the exact laws of the greater causes, and of such of the minor ones as are sufficiently known, with such empirical laws or such approximate generalizations respecting the miscellaneous variations as can be obtained by specific observation, we can lay down general propositions which will be true in the main.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It is acceptable and often necessary in moral/social inquiry to mix rigorous general laws (where available) with empirical, approximate generalizations about less-understood influences; but always allow for probable inaccuracy when grounding expectations or conduct on such combined laws.

rubrics_metrics.name: Adapt natural-science methods to moral and social inquiry with stricter induction
rubrics_metrics.description: If the laws of Mind, and ... those of Society, are to be made subjects of science, the same process through which the laws of many simpler phenomena have been placed beyond dispute must be consciously and deliberately applied to those more difficult inquiries.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Examine which existing methods are especially suited to branches of moral inquiry, under what peculiar facilities or difficulties they are employed, and whether unsatisfactory results stem from wrong choice of methods or poor application of right ones. Moral sciences require stricter rules of induction than are commonly recognized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not construct methods in isolation — exemplification is required
rubrics_metrics.description: In attempting this, I am not unmindful how little can be done toward it in a mere treatise on Logic, or how vague and unsatisfactory all precepts of Method must necessarily appear when not practically exemplified in the establishment of a body of doctrine.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological prescriptions should be illustrated by constructing theories or bodies of doctrine; otherwise rules remain abstract and of limited use. Use historical and practical exemplars (e.g., Bacon) to show how methods work in practice.

rubrics_metrics.name: Predictive limits for individual human behavior due to incomplete data and idiosyncratic history
rubrics_metrics.description: The actions of individuals could not be predicted with scientific accuracy ... because we can not foresee the whole of the circumstances in which those individuals will be placed ... and the agencies which determine human character are so numerous and diversified that in the aggregate they are never in any two cases exactly similar.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Recognize the theoretical possibility of precise prediction if complete data were available, but accept the practical impossibility due to unknown/unique antecedents. Therefore avoid claiming universal, precise laws about individual behavior.

rubrics_metrics.name: Focus on general causes common to large groups for reliable predictions
rubrics_metrics.description: Many of those effects which it is of most importance to render amenable to human foresight and control are determined ... in the main by those circumstances and qualities which are common to all mankind, or at least to large bodies of them, and only in a small degree on the idiosyncrasies of organization or the peculiar history of individuals.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For useful social-scientific prediction and policy, identify and study the general causes that predominate across populations; such predictions will 'almost always' be verified despite individual irregularities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use precise terminology to avoid misleading associations (avoid 'Necessity')
rubrics_metrics.description: The application of so improper a term as Necessity to the doctrine of cause and effect in the matter of human character, seems to me one of the most signal instances in philosophy of the abuse of terms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid terms that carry extraneous emotional or metaphysical connotations (e.g., 'necessity' implying irresistibleness or fatalism). Prefer clearer expressions about causation, predictability, and the conditional character of outcomes to prevent confusion in debates about freedom and determinism.

rubrics_metrics.name: Causation of human actions: include motives, character, purposes, and habitual willing
rubrics_metrics.description: Correctly conceived, the doctrine ... is that, given the motives which are present to an individual’s mind, and given likewise the character and disposition of the individual, the manner in which he will act might be unerringly inferred ... Among the causes of our volitions ... must be reckoned not only likings and aversions, but also purposes.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When explaining or predicting behavior, account for motives (including non-conscious or habitual motives), settled purposes, and the individual's character. Recognize that habits and purposes may persist even after the original pleasure/pain motives have ceased.

rubrics_metrics.name: Account for reciprocal influence: individuals can partly form their own character
rubrics_metrics.description: His character is formed by his circumstances ... but his own desire to mould it in a particular way, is one of those circumstances ... We are exactly as capable of making our own character, if we will, as others are of making it for us.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Methodological accounts of human behavior should include feedback loops: individuals influence their future circumstances and character via intentional acts; analyses that treat character as wholly externally formed will be incomplete and may have demotivating practical consequences.
